 ‘Human connection is more important than ever’: How to fight holiday stress
 By Kate Ryan 
 November 7, 2026 | 
 4:18 AM 
 | 
 For some, the season of family gatherings and holiday gift-giving creates a surge of excitement, but for others, the looming holidays can generate a season of stress.
 Frayed family relations can be strained further when there are political differences hanging over the holiday table, and coming off the midterms, that may be a real source of tension.

 “You can’t control how other people behave, you can’t control the outcome of the election, but you can control how you interact with people, how you decide to focus your time and energy,” Heather Hartman-Hall , a psychologist at MedStar Health and senior director for wellbeing and mental health at MedStar’s Center for Wellbeing, told WTOP. “The holidays are about things that we care about. So if you can focus on the things that really bring meaning, that will help you know where to put your energy.”
 Social calendars tend to get packed, from November right up through New Year’s, so Hartman-Hall said that if it gets to be too much, then do not be afraid to say no to some things, or set boundaries. She said that you don’t have to feel like you have to do it all.
 “You have to focus on the things that are truly most important to you,” Hartman-Hall said.
 Another source of stress can come from trying to pick the perfect gifts for family and friends while trying to stick to a budget. 
 “Finances are a real stressor for a lot of people right now,” Hartman-Hall said. “Finding ways to make the holidays about meaningful connection, a small, thoughtful gift can have a really big impact.”
 Sometimes, the gift of time can be the best present, according to Hartman-Hall. Carving out time for a special activity and be meaningful. 
 “Human connection is more important than ever,” she said. “I think a meaningful, thoughtful gift or even activity or time together can go a long way and doesn’t need to cost a lot of money.”

 With an ode to mate, pope urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
 By The Associated Press 
 November 7, 2026 | 
 9:05 AM 
 | 
 PAYSANDÚ, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, as he used his first Mass in South America to deliver an ode to the region's beloved mate tea and raise the profile of the Catholic Church in its most secular country.
The crowd erupted in the stadium chant of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Pope, Pope!” when Leo's plane landed in Paysandú, in western Uruguay on the border with Argentina. They cheered again, blew horns and waved yellow handkerchiefs when he arrived in his open-sided popemobile at the Mass site in the Parque París Londres, a sprawling green space on the southern edge of Paysandú.
More than 30,000 people — many from Uruguay but also from neighboring Argentina and Brazil — had registered in advance to attend the service, around 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said Saturday another 10,000 had shown up beyond that, despite the morning rain and blustery, gray skies.
Because of its accessible location on the Uruguay River, the city was chosen to host Leo’s first Mass at the start of his three-nation South American tour that was in doubt after he underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13.
